summary: Defines a MIB module for devices doing Network Address Translation, usable for both configuring and monitoring them. It was replaced by RFC 7658.

eli5.summary: A set of dials for checking and setting up a box that swaps addresses on network traffic. A newer document replaced it.

subtitle: An SNMP MIB module for configuring and monitoring devices that do Network Address Translation.

tldr.problem: Operators had no standard way to configure and monitor the NAT function of a device over SNMP.
tldr.mechanism: The NAT-MIB module defines tables for NAT interfaces, address maps, address binds, port binds and sessions, plus default timeouts and a packet-discard notification.
tldr.outcome: Devices can be managed through a common set of objects. The module was later obsoleted by RFC 7658.

facts.label: NAT service types
facts.value: Basic NAT, NAPT, twice NAT, bidirectional NAT

today: RFC 4008 was a Proposed Standard published in March 2005 and has been obsoleted by RFC 7658, which is now the place to look for this MIB.

sections.title: Scope of the NAT MIB
sections.content:
RFC 4008 defines a portion of the Management Information Base (MIB) for devices that perform Network Address Translation. The module can be used for both configuration and monitoring. NAT types are defined in RFC 2663 and traditional NAT in RFC 3022.

The MIB does not address firewall functions and MUST NOT be used to configure or monitor them. Objects are accessed through SNMP and defined with SMIv2. NAT sessions are limited to TCP and UDP, with other transports such as SCTP, UDP-lite and DCCP left for possible future extension.
sections.eli5: It covers the address-swapping part of a box, and not the part that blocks bad traffic.

sections.title: Realms, Binds and Sessions
sections.content:
An address realm is a set of unique, routable addresses, for example private addresses inside an enterprise or the globally unique public realm. Each NAT interface is connected to either a private or a public realm.

A bind is either an Address Bind, a tuple of private and public IP address, or a Port Bind, a tuple of transport protocol, private address and port, and public address and port. A NAT session ties together a session as seen in the private realm with the same session as seen in the public realm.

Address maps are static or dynamic. Each static bind has a one-to-one relationship with a static address map entry, while dynamic binds are created from a dynamic map entry when the first packet of a new session is seen.
sections.eli5: A bind is a pen-pal list pairing a private name with a public name. A session is one conversation using that pairing.

sections.title: The Tables
sections.content:
Configuration starts with natInterfaceTable, indexed by ifIndex. It sets the interface realm type (private or public) and the NAT services enabled: Basic NAT, NAPT, twice NAT and bidirectional NAT. natAddrMapTable, indexed by interface and map index, holds address maps. NAT looks up map entries in the order defined to choose the translation at the start of each new session.

The operator must pick map entries to suit the interface. For a NAPT map on a public interface the translation entity should be outboundSrcEndPoint, and on a private interface InboundSrcEndPoint.

natAddrBindTable and natAddrPortBindTable hold binds, and natSessionTable holds sessions. These are derived from the maps and are not configurable. A bind must not exist without an address map entry, and, except for symmetric NAT, a session must not exist without a bind. A natProtocolTable keeps per-protocol statistics.
sections.eli5: You choose the doors (interfaces) and write the rules (maps). The box fills in the lists of pairings and conversations by itself, and you can only read those.

sections.title: Configuration, Timeouts and NAT Variations
sections.content:
A management station creates an entry in natInterfaceTable, then creates one or more address map entries in reducing order of priority, and finally sets the maximum idle time for binds and for TCP, UDP and ICMP sessions in natDefTimeouts. Those timeouts are global, not per interface.

The MIB does not name the NAPT variations of RFC 3489, but they can be told apart from the bind and session objects. A Port Restricted Cone NAT has non-zero bind ids and no wildcards. Address Restricted Cone and Full Cone NATs may use zero (match anything) values for destination address and port objects in UDP sessions. A Symmetric NAT keeps no port binds, so its bind tables are empty and its session bind id is zero.

The natPacketDiscard notification reports packets discarded for lack of address mappings. The natNotifThrottlingInterval object (0 or 5 to 3600 seconds, default 0, meaning off) limits how often it is generated.
sections.eli5: You set how long to remember an idle pairing, and the box can send an alert when it drops traffic it had no rule for, but not too often.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
No security holes were identified beyond those SNMP security itself addresses. Bind and session objects reveal which private hosts are talking to outside nodes, so a curious outsider could count the hosts behind the NAT, and a former insider could use the information to attack specific hosts. It may be important to control GET access to these objects and encrypt them.

SNMP versions before SNMPv3 did not include adequate security. The RFC says deploying them is NOT RECOMMENDED, and RECOMMENDS SNMPv3 with cryptographic security and careful access control.
sections.eli5: The lists show who is talking to whom, so only trusted people should be allowed to look, and the lock on the control panel should be strong.
